extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal researchers, and practitioners researching Florida administrative law and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A research guide for locating, understanding, and verifying Florida administrative rules, associated statutes, agency actions, and adjudicative records (DOAH). Focuses on primary sources (FAC/FAR), statutory authority, rulemaking procedure under Chapter 120, and research tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official source for administrative rules (FAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The online Florida Administrative Code (FAC) is the official version of administrative rules for Florida.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the FAC as the authoritative text of agency rules. The guide links to multiple vendors and official sources (Online FAC, Lexis FAC, Bloomberg FAC, Westlaw FAC, F.A.L.C.O.N.) to view the current regulatory text. Prefer the official FAC when citing or evaluating rule language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Florida Administrative Register (FAR) as rulemaking status source
rubrics_metrics.description: Florida Administrative Register (FAR) is the daily publication which gives the current information about the status of rules moving through the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAR includes proposed rules, emergency rules, notices of change, corrections and withdrawals and notices of agency public meetings, workshops and hearings, and miscellaneous actions. Use FAR to identify open comment periods, upcoming hearings, emergency rule notices, and recent amendments in process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional databases and tracking tools for FAC/FAR
rubrics_metrics.description: Databases and regulation-tracking services provide access to FAC/FAR and tracking for changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools mentioned include F.A.L.C.O.N., Lexis FAC and FAR, Lexis Advance Regulation Tracking, Bloomberg FAC, Westlaw FAC, and Westlaw Fla Regulation Tracking. Use these platforms to search, track regulatory developments, and retrieve historical versions or related materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority requirement for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for an agency to make a rule, the agency must be authorized by law to take the action specified in the rule and to engage in rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that the agency cites a statutory grant of rulemaking power and that the content of the rule falls within that delegation. If an agency acts without statutory authorization, its action may be subject to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific authority (statute authorizing rulemaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific authority is the law which states that the agency can make a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the rule's statutory citations for a 'specific authority' clause (example given: s. 1001.74(4) provided authority for the Florida Department of Education rule). Confirm the statute's text and any limitations on delegated power before relying on the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law implemented (substantive statute the rule expands or clarifies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law implemented is the substantive law which the rule will expand on or clarify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the statute the rule is intended to implement (example: s. 1001.74(10)). Ensure the rule's provisions are a permissible interpretation or implementation of that statute rather than introducing requirements beyond the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace a rule back to the governing statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: 'How to go from a rule to a statute' by identifying the types of statutory authority cited on the rule (specific authority and law implemented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching a rule, use the rule's header/citation information to locate the enabling statute(s). This helps assess scope, limits, and whether the agency properly relied on statutory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter 120 (Florida APA) procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 120, in Florida Statutes, is the Administrative Procedures Act which describes the rulemaking process for Florida's agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 120 procedures involve publishing proposed rules, accepting and responding to public comment, and following prescribed notice and hearing processes. Confirm agencies have followed Chapter 120 steps; failure to do so or action not supported by a formal rule or law may be challenged as beyond delegated authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DOAH records to review adjudicative proceedings and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: A person affected by an agency's decision can appeal the decision to the Division of Administrative Hearings (DOAH). DOAH issues a Recommended Order to the agency. The agency then issues a Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult DOAH's website (Case Search) to view filings and recommended orders; DOAH often provides access to almost all case filings, not just recommended orders found on commercial services. Use DOAH records to understand legal challenges, factual records, and agency reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate and consult agency websites and snapshots
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding an agency website helps locate agency-specific rulemaking materials, notices, and meeting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the guide's 'List of Florida agencies' and 'Agency snapshots' links to find agency pages that post rule notices, meeting agendas, supporting documents, and contact information. Agency sites can provide materials not centrally published elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult secondary/practice resources for interpretation and practice guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary sources and practice materials explain administrative law practice and rulemaking nuances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources listed include Florida Administrative Practice (Lexis print and online), FALCON/JAPC FAQ, and Admin Law Section of the Florida Bar newsletters. Use these for doctrinal context, procedural guidance, common pitfalls, and practitioner-oriented explanations when evaluating rules or preparing comments/challenges.
